analogy.p: Think of each type of EM wave as a different key and each material as a lock. Water molecules in food are 'locked' by microwaves, so only microwaves are absorbed strongly and heat the food; bone is 'locked' by X-rays but soft tissue is not, so X-rays make a picture of bones. Glass lets visible light through but not much else, so it suits fibre optics. The analogy breaks down because absorption is not all-or-nothing: most materials absorb a range of wavelengths by different amounts, and the spectrum is continuous, not a few separate keys.
analogy.t: A set of keys and locks

bullets: Uses required: **radio** (television and radio), **microwaves** (satellite communications, cooking food), **infrared** (electrical heaters, cooking food, infrared cameras), **visible light** (fibre optic communications), **ultraviolet** (energy efficient lamps, sun tanning), **X-rays and gamma rays** (medical imaging and treatments).
Hazards required: **UV** (premature ageing of skin, increased risk of skin cancer); **X-rays and gamma rays** (ionising radiation which can cause **mutation of genes and cancer**).

**Radiation dose** is a measure of the **risk of harm** from exposure of the body to radiation; it is measured in **sieverts (Sv)**; **1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv)**. You do not need to recall the unit name, but you must be able to use it when given.
The effects depend on **both the type of radiation and the size of the dose**; always mention both when asked.
Command words: 'give a use' needs the use; 'explain why suitable' needs the **property** linked to the use (the 'because' part earns the mark).
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: This spec point links the **properties** of each EM wave to its **practical uses**, and then to the **dangers** of the high-frequency end of the spectrum. You must be able to give a brief explanation of **why each type of wave is suitable** for each application, not just state the use. You also need to know that the **effects of radiation depend on the type of radiation and the size of the dose**, that **radiation dose is measured in sieverts (Sv)**, and that UV, X-rays and gamma rays are hazardous to human tissue. The whole topic rests on one idea: waves interact with matter differently depending on wavelength, so each part of the spectrum suits a different job.

bullets: **Why radio for TV and radio:** very little absorbed by the atmosphere, so signals travel far; they can pass through or round buildings; they are **not harmful** to people at normal broadcast levels.
Different stations use **different frequencies**, so a receiver can be **tuned** to pick one frequency and reject others.
Wavelength range is large: from roughly **0.1 m to more than 10 km**; the longer the wavelength, the more the wave tends to bend round obstacles.

**Extension:** some radio waves (longer wavelength, lower frequency) are **reflected by the ionosphere**, which lets them be received over very long distances; the higher-frequency waves used for TV and FM go in straight lines (line of sight) and need a chain of transmitters.
Speed in air is about **3.0 x 10^8 m/s**, so the wave equation **v = f x wavelength** gives wavelength from frequency (e.g. a 94.0 MHz FM station: wavelength = 3.0 x 10^8 / 9.4 x 10^7 = 3.2 m).

Radio waves can be **produced by oscillations in electrical circuits** and **induce** an alternating current of the same frequency when absorbed (Higher tier idea, covered in detail in its own spec point).
core.p: Radio waves have the **longest wavelengths** and **lowest frequencies** of the EM spectrum, so they carry the least energy per wave. Transmitters make them by an **alternating current** in an aerial, and a receiver aerial absorbs them to produce a matching alternating current that is turned into sound or picture. They suit broadcasting because they can travel **long distances**, pass through the air with **very little absorption**, and the long-wavelength ones **diffract** (spread) around hills and buildings, so many homes can receive the signal without a direct view of the transmitter.

bullets: **Why microwaves for satellites:** they can pass through the **atmosphere** (including the ionosphere that reflects some radio waves) to reach space and come back.
Their short wavelength means they can be sent as a **narrow, focused beam** from a dish, so less energy is wasted.
A satellite **receives** the microwave signal, **amplifies** it, and **retransmits** it to a receiving dish elsewhere on Earth.

Delay: the signal travels at **3.0 x 10^8 m/s**; for a satellite about 3.6 x 10^7 m above the ground the one-way time is 3.6 x 10^7 / 3.0 x 10^8 = **0.12 s**, which is why satellite phone calls can have a noticeable delay.
Link: the same wave equation **v = f x wavelength** and **speed = distance / time** apply to all EM waves.
Microwaves of a different wavelength are strongly absorbed by water; the frequencies chosen for satellite communication are ones that the atmosphere does **not** absorb strongly.
core.p: Microwaves have shorter wavelengths than radio waves (roughly millimetres to tens of centimetres). The **microwaves used for satellite communication pass through the atmosphere** without being significantly absorbed or reflected, so a signal can travel from a **ground station up to a satellite** and be sent back down to another place. Satellite TV, satellite phones and satnav (GPS) all rely on this. The signal is **transmitted as a narrow beam** from a dish aimed at the satellite.

bullets: **Why microwaves for cooking:** the wavelength is strongly absorbed by **water molecules** in food, which makes cooking fast and efficient.
Energy transfer: electrical energy store of the oven, to the magnetron which makes microwaves, to the **thermal energy store** of the food.
Dry or frozen foods heat poorly because there is little **liquid water** free to absorb the energy (ice absorbs much less well).
The myth 'cooks from the inside out' is wrong: absorption is mainly in the **outer layers**; heat then spreads inwards by conduction.
**Danger:** microwaves can **heat body tissue** (internal heating of cells), which is why the oven door has a safety interlock and a metal screen.
Microwaves do **not** make food radioactive and are **non-ionising**; the risk is heating, not mutation.
core.p: A microwave oven uses microwaves of a wavelength that is **absorbed by water, fat and sugar molecules** in food. The absorbed energy is transferred to the **thermal energy store** of those molecules, so their kinetic energy increases and the food heats up. The energy is absorbed in the **outer few centimetres** of the food; the rest then warms by **conduction** (and by convection in liquids). Metal walls and the metal mesh in the door **reflect** microwaves so they stay inside the oven and bounce around until absorbed.

bullets: **Heaters:** a hot element emits infrared which is **absorbed by the surroundings and people**, increasing their thermal energy.
**Cooking:** grills and toasters use infrared to heat the **surface** of the food directly.
**Infrared cameras (thermal imaging):** show temperature differences; used for **night vision**, finding people in rescue work, security, and spotting **heat loss from buildings**.
**Why infrared:** it is emitted by everything warm, so cameras need no light source; it is readily **absorbed** by surfaces, so it is good at heating them.
Also used (example beyond the list): **remote controls** and short-range data links.
**Danger:** too much infrared absorbed by skin causes **burns**; it is non-ionising, so it does not cause gene mutation.
Link: black surfaces are good absorbers and good emitters of infrared (black body radiation topic).
core.h: Infrared: heaters, cooking and infrared cameras
core.p: **All objects emit infrared radiation**, and the **hotter** an object is, the **more infrared** it emits (and the shorter the mean wavelength). When a surface **absorbs** infrared, the energy goes to its thermal store and its temperature rises. This explains electrical heaters, grills and toasters: a very hot element emits lots of infrared, which is absorbed by the food or by people and objects in the room. An **infrared camera** works in the opposite direction: it detects the infrared emitted by objects and converts it to a visible image, so warmer objects look brighter or are shown in a different colour.

bullets: **Why light suits fibres:** it is **transmitted through glass** with very little absorption, so signals travel far before needing a booster.
High frequency means a large **amount of information** can be carried quickly (high data rate).
Advantages over copper wire: **faster, more capacity, little interference**, harder to tap, thinner and lighter cables.
Signals are sent as **digital pulses** (on and off), which are easy to regenerate cleanly.
Other uses: **photography**, seeing, illumination, and **endoscopes** that use bundles of fibres to look inside the body.
**Extension:** total internal reflection happens when light in the glass hits the boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle; you only need to say light is 'reflected along the fibre'.
core.p: Visible light is the only part of the spectrum our **eyes can detect**. In **fibre optic cables**, digital signals are sent as **pulses of light (or infrared) down thin glass or plastic fibres**. The light is repeatedly reflected off the inside wall of the fibre (**total internal reflection**) so it follows the fibre even round bends. Fibre optics carry telephone, TV and internet signals.

bullets: **Energy efficient lamps:** UV is made inside the tube, absorbed by the coating, and converted to **visible light**, with less energy wasted as thermal energy.
**Why UV suits tanning:** UV is absorbed by skin and triggers melanin production, giving the tanned appearance.
Other uses: **security marking** (invisible ink glows under UV), sterilising water, and checking banknotes.
UV has enough energy to damage cells: **premature ageing** of the skin and an increased risk of **skin cancer**.
Reduce risk with **sunscreen**, covering up, shade and limiting time in strong sun or on sunbeds.
UV from the Sun is mostly absorbed by the **ozone layer**; darker skin has more melanin and so more natural protection.
core.h: Ultraviolet: energy efficient lamps and sun tanning
core.p: Ultraviolet (UV) has **higher frequency and shorter wavelength than visible light**, so it carries more energy per wave. In an **energy efficient (fluorescent) lamp**, an electrical discharge makes **mercury vapour** emit UV. The UV is absorbed by a **phosphor coating** on the inside of the tube, which re-emits the energy as **visible light** (**fluorescence**). This wastes less energy as heat than a filament lamp, so the lamp is more efficient. In **sun tanning**, UV makes skin cells produce the dark pigment **melanin**, which absorbs UV and gives some protection; tanning beds produce UV artificially.

bullets: **Why X-rays suit imaging:** they pass through soft tissue but are **absorbed by bone**, giving contrast.
**Why they suit treatment:** high-energy X-rays can **destroy cancer cells**; the beam is aimed from several directions to limit damage to healthy tissue.
X-rays are produced when **fast electrons hit a metal target** in an X-ray tube.
They are **ionising radiation**: they can remove electrons from atoms, damage DNA, and cause cancer.
**Protection:** radiographers stand behind **lead screens** or leave the room; patients may wear **lead aprons**; exposure time and dose are kept as **low as possible**.
Barium meals contain dense barium, which absorbs X-rays and lets the gut show up on the image.
core.p: X-rays have very short wavelengths and high frequencies. They are **transmitted by soft tissue** but **absorbed by dense materials such as bone and metal**. In an X-ray image, X-rays pass from a tube through the patient to a **detector (photographic film or digital sensor)**. Where X-rays reach the detector it darkens; where bone absorbed them it stays pale. This gives a **shadow picture of bones** to show fractures or dental problems. **CT scans** combine many X-ray images to build 3D pictures. At higher doses, X-rays can **kill cancer cells** (radiotherapy).

bullets: **Why gamma suits tracers:** gamma rays pass **out of the body** and can be detected by a camera, while alpha and beta cannot.
Tracers have a **short half-life** (e.g. hours) so the activity falls quickly and the patient's dose is small.
**Treatment:** gamma damages DNA in cancer cells so they cannot divide; beams from different angles meet at the tumour to protect healthy tissue.
**Sterilising:** gamma kills bacteria on equipment sealed in packaging, with no heating.
**Difference from X-rays:** gamma rays come from the **nucleus**; X-rays are made by electrons. The two ranges overlap in frequency.
Gamma is **ionising** and causes mutation and cancer; handle with shielding (thick lead or concrete), distance and short time.
core.h: Gamma rays: medical imaging and treatments
core.p: Gamma rays have the **shortest wavelengths and highest frequencies** in the spectrum and are emitted by **unstable atomic nuclei** during radioactive decay. They are very penetrating, so they can pass through the body. In **medical imaging**, a patient swallows or is injected with a **gamma-emitting tracer** with a short half-life; a **gamma camera** outside the body detects where the gamma rays come from and shows how organs are working. In **treatment**, a narrow beam of gamma rays aimed at a tumour from several directions can **kill cancer cells**. Gamma is also used to **sterilise surgical instruments and food**.

bullets: **Low-frequency waves** (radio, microwave, infrared, visible) are non-ionising: they cannot knock electrons off atoms, so they do not cause gene mutation. They can still cause **heating** or burns at high intensity.
**UV** can damage skin cells: **premature ageing** and **increased risk of skin cancer**; also can harm eyes.
**X-rays and gamma rays** are **ionising radiation** which can **mutate genes** and cause **cancer**; very large doses kill cells and cause radiation sickness.
Dose conversion example: **0.25 mSv = 0.25 / 1000 = 0.00025 Sv**; **0.3 Sv = 300 mSv**.
Higher-frequency waves are more dangerous because each wave carries **more energy**, enough to ionise atoms.
Risk is about **probability**: a small dose slightly raises the chance of harm, but does not mean harm will definitely occur.
core.p: The harm caused by a type of radiation depends on **how much energy it carries** and on the **size of the dose**. **Radiation dose** is a **measure of the risk of harm** from exposure to radiation, measured in **sieverts (Sv)**; because the sievert is large, doctors usually use **millisieverts (mSv)**, where **1000 mSv = 1 Sv**. A larger dose means a larger risk. The dose also depends on the type of radiation, because some types damage tissue much more than others.

bullets: Step by step: **ionising radiation is absorbed**, then **atoms are ionised**, then **DNA is damaged**, then a **gene mutation** can occur, then **uncontrolled division** can lead to **cancer**.
Cells that divide often (skin, gut lining, bone marrow) are more affected.
High doses can kill many cells at once, causing **radiation sickness**; low doses mostly increase **long-term cancer risk**.
Damage to **sex cells** could lead to mutations passed on to children.
This is why X-rays and gamma rays both **help treat** cancer (killing tumour cells) and **can cause** cancer (mutating healthy cells).
Do not say 'radiation makes you radioactive': being **irradiated** is different from being **contaminated**.
core.h: Ionisation and why mutation leads to cancer
core.p: **Ionisation** is when radiation has enough energy to **remove electrons from atoms or molecules**, forming **ions**. If this happens in a living cell, it can damage the **DNA** in the nucleus. A damaged gene may be repaired, may cause the cell to die, or may be **mutated**: a changed base sequence copied when the cell divides. If a mutation affects the genes that control cell division, the cell can divide **uncontrollably**, forming a **tumour**: cancer.

bullets: **Reducing dose:** short exposure time, a **narrow beam** aimed only at the area needed, **lead shielding** for other body parts, and staff **behind screens**.
**Monitoring:** radiographers wear **film badges** that darken when exposed to radiation, so their dose can be checked.
**Pregnancy:** unborn babies are very sensitive, so X-rays are avoided unless essential.
Evaluate with **numbers** where given: compare doses in mSv and say which is larger and by how many times.
Society may weigh **benefit** (early diagnosis, saved lives) against **risk** (small chance of cancer later); both must be mentioned in a 6-mark answer.
Scientists publish and peer review dose studies so decisions are based on **evidence**.
core.h: Weighing risks and benefits; keeping doses low
core.p: Medical use of ionising radiation is justified when the **benefit outweighs the risk**: a diagnosis or a cancer treatment is worth a small increase in cancer risk. Doses are kept **as low as reasonably possible**. Staff who work with radiation wear **film badges or dosimeters** to monitor their total dose, and the patient dose in a scan is very small compared with the dose that kills cells.

bullets: **Radio:** long wavelength, low absorption, diffracts, so reaches many receivers.
**Microwave (satellite):** passes through the atmosphere; **(cooking):** absorbed by water in food.
**Infrared:** emitted by warm objects; absorbed by surfaces, so it heats.
**Visible:** transmitted through glass fibres; seen by the eye.
**UV:** absorbed by phosphor coatings to give visible light; absorbed by skin to cause melanin production.
**X-rays:** absorbed by bone, transmitted by soft tissue. **Gamma:** penetrates the body, emitted by tracers, kills cells.
**Common error:** writing that a wave is used 'because it is strong' or 'because it is fast'. All EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum.
core.h: Matching property to use: the reasoning that earns marks
core.p: Mark schemes want a **property** and a **consequence**. Properties to use are: how strongly the wave is **absorbed** by a material, whether it is **transmitted** through it, **reflected** by it, or **refracted**, the **wavelength** (diffraction, beam width), the **frequency** (energy carried, data rate), and whether it is **ionising**. A good answer says 'X is used for Y **because** it is absorbed/transmitted by Z'.

bullets: Use **standard form**, state units, and check that frequency is in **Hz** (1 MHz = 10^6 Hz) before using the wave equation.
Graph or table questions: say which has the **greatest dose** and compare using figures, e.g. 'twice as large'.
Link to **half-life**: tracers need a short half-life so the patient is irradiated for a shorter time.
Link to **energy transfers**: microwave oven transfers electrical energy to the thermal store of food.
Link to **absorption**: the same wave can be transmitted by one material and absorbed by another.
Link to **sound/ultrasound**: sound is longitudinal and needs a medium; EM waves are transverse and travel in a vacuum.
Link to **Earth's atmosphere**: the ozone layer absorbs UV; the atmosphere is transparent to visible, radio and some microwave.
core.h: Data skills and links to other topics
core.p: Exam questions often give data such as doses, frequencies or wavelengths and ask you to compare or calculate. Remember **v = f x wavelength** with **v = 3.0 x 10^8 m/s**; **mSv to Sv by dividing by 1000**; and compare risks by giving figures. Link this topic to atomic structure (ionisation), radioactivity (gamma emission, half-life, tracers), energy stores (microwave and infrared heating), and the EM spectrum properties point.

exam: **State/Give (1 mark):** name the use or hazard, e.g. 'skin cancer', 'satellite communications'.
**Explain why suitable (2 marks):** one property + consequence, e.g. 'microwaves pass through the atmosphere so signals reach the satellite'.
**Describe (3-4 marks):** step by step; use words like 'absorbed', 'transmitted', 'reflected', 'detected'.
**Hazard questions:** always name the **type** of radiation and the **effect**: 'UV causes skin cancer; X-rays and gamma cause gene mutation and cancer'.
**Dose answers:** mention the **size of the dose** as well as the type of radiation; give unit sievert/millisievert correctly.
**6-mark evaluate:** give benefits (diagnosis, treatment) AND risks (ionisation, cancer), compare using figures, and end with a justified conclusion.
**Calculations:** write the equation, substitute with correct units (convert MHz to Hz, mSv to Sv), show working, give answer with unit.
**Do not** say gamma and X-rays 'burn' you or 'make you radioactive'; use ionising/mutate wording.
**Matching table questions:** learn the list of uses exactly as in the specification.
**Diagram questions:** label source, patient/bone, detector; state that bone appears white because less X-ray reaches the detector.

mistakes.r: X-rays are transmitted by soft tissue but absorbed by dense bone, which creates the contrast in the image.
mistakes.w: X-rays are used because they can see through everything.

mistakes.r: Microwaves are absorbed by water in the outer few centimetres; the heat then conducts inwards.
mistakes.w: Microwaves cook from the inside out.

mistakes.r: Microwaves are non-ionising and do not make anything radioactive; the effect is heating.
Infrared is a wave; when absorbed it increases the thermal energy store of the object, which causes heating.
Effects depend on the type of radiation and the size of the dose; X-rays and gamma are ionising and mutate genes; UV causes skin ageing and skin cancer.
mistakes.w: UV, X-rays and gamma all cause cancer in the same way and amount.

mistakes.r: Gamma rays are a form of radiation emitted by radioactive nuclei; the source is radioactive, the ray is not.
They carry pulses of light (or infrared) by reflection along the fibre.
Radio waves are transverse EM waves; sound waves are longitudinal and need a medium.
Dose in sieverts is a measure of risk; a larger dose of any harmful radiation means greater risk.
mistakes.w: A big dose means a high chance of harm only if it is gamma.

summary: You must link each type of EM wave to its practical uses (radio, microwaves, infrared, visible light, UV, X-rays and gamma rays) and explain why each is suitable, then describe the hazards of UV, X-rays and gamma rays and how radiation dose (in sieverts) measures the risk of harm. It matters because exam questions ask you to explain why a wave suits a job and to weigh up benefits and risks.

terms.d: A transverse wave that transfers energy from a source to an absorber and can travel through a vacuum at 3.0 x 10^8 m/s.
EM waves with the longest wavelengths and lowest frequencies; used for television and radio.
EM waves used for satellite communications and cooking food.
EM radiation emitted by all objects; used in heaters, cooking and infrared cameras.
The part of the spectrum detected by the eye; used in fibre optic communications.
EM waves of higher frequency than visible light; used in energy efficient lamps and sun tanning; can cause skin cancer.
High-frequency EM waves transmitted by soft tissue and absorbed by bone; used in medical imaging and treatments.
The highest-frequency EM waves, emitted by nuclei; used in medical imaging and treatments.
Radiation with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, e.g. X-rays and gamma rays.
The process of an atom gaining or losing electrons to become an ion.
A change to the sequence of a gene (DNA) which may lead to cancer.
A measure of the risk of harm from exposure of the body to radiation, in sieverts.
The unit of radiation dose; 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert.
A thin glass or plastic fibre that carries light signals by repeated reflection.
Absorbing UV and re-emitting the energy as visible light, as in an energy efficient lamp.
A radioactive substance that emits gamma rays, put into the body to show how an organ works.
Making a picture from the infrared emitted by objects, so hotter objects look brighter.
When a wave transfers its energy to the material it meets.

worked.ans: X-rays pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by bone, so the bone appears as a pale shadow on the detector and a fracture can be seen. Radiographers leave the room because X-rays are ionising radiation which can mutate genes and cause cancer, and their dose would build up over time.
worked.q: Explain why X-rays are used to take images of broken bones and why radiographers leave the room. (4 marks)
steps: Mark 1: X-rays are transmitted by soft tissue.
Mark 2: X-rays are absorbed by dense bone.
Mark 3: So less X-ray reaches the detector behind the bone, which shows as a pale area, so the break can be seen.
Mark 4: X-rays are ionising and can cause gene mutation and cancer, so repeated exposure of staff is a risk.
